clue.text: Company discovered change into a solid base

parts.note: a firm is a business company
to have found something is to have discovered it
taken as written, as anagram material

indicators.note: change tells us to rework the letters of the two little words that follow it

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A business has found that a transformation will put it on a sound footing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discovered' looks like part of the surface story but supplies a synonym; 'change' anagrams only the two short words beside it, giving ATION.
explanation.definitionFit: A stable grounding for anything is figuratively a solid base, the literal footing of a building.

clue.text: Fool using a sumo ring — that's out of order

indicators.note: out of order says the letters of the preceding phrase are not in their proper sequence

parts.note: taken as written, nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone stepping into a wrestling ring the wrong way is called an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of order' is the anagram signal applied to A SUMO RING.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignorant, foolish person is a fool; the Latin-derived word is a straight synonym.

parts.note: a chap is a man
to go is to leave

explanation.surface: A fellow must abandon some fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A tropical stone fruit, so an example of the general category of fruit.

clue.text: balls wildly wrong? It's got too much

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled from one end

indicators.note: wildly says the letters of the next word are thrown about

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A cricketer's deliveries spraying everywhere suggest someone with an excess of something.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six deliveries, so 'balls' is not a plural of ball here; 'wildly' anagrams the next word into GROWN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has grown excessively, say a garden, has developed too much, the sense here.

clue.text: Close to time for period of darkness

parts.note: nigh is an old word meaning near or close to

explanation.surface: Approaching the hour when darkness falls.
explanation.definitionFit: The hours between sunset and sunrise are the dark part of each day.

parts.note: a cellar is a basement, a room below ground level

explanation.surface: Being sent down to the cellar is treated as a step down in rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Being lowered in rank or esteem is a humbling, the same idea as a demotion.

clue.text: At home, long for independent record company

parts.note: in means at home, as in 'staying in'
to be dying for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: Staying in and yearning for a small music label.
explanation.walkthrough: DIE for 'long for' comes from the idiom 'dying for a drink'.
explanation.definitionFit: A small record label not owned by a major is called by this short form of independent.

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: rate is a speed, as in a rate of knots

explanation.surface: After sprinting quickly, someone gives an account.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'up' means reading upwards, giving NAR; 'speed' supplies its synonym afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To recount or tell a story is to give a report of it, a verb synonym.

parts.note: c is an abbreviation for cycle, as in cycles per second
left means abandoned, as in left behind
S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A bike left lying about on little cracks in the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Cracks or splits in rock are fissures, synonyms of crevices.

parts.note: a line is a crease or wrinkle

explanation.surface: Ironing a fold into freshly bought bedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Bed sheets are traditionally made from flax cloth, so the fabric names the bedding collectively.

clue.text: A Brit, from country covered in unusual green

indicators.note: covered in says one piece is wrapped inside another
unusual says the letters of the next word appear in an odd order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material
land is a nation or country

explanation.surface: A British person comes from a land carpeted in strange greenery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' scrambles the colour into ENGER, and 'covered in' tells you the country sits inside that scramble rather than beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the largest UK nation is a Briton, so this inhabitant name fits a Brit.

clue.text: Animal skins get extended for 220 yards

parts.note: fur is the hairy pelt of animals
long means extended in length

explanation.surface: Animal pelts are stretched out to cover a set distance.
explanation.definitionFit: This old unit of length, an eighth of a mile, is exactly two hundred and twenty yards, still used in horse racing.

parts.note: yonder means over there

explanation.surface: That lady over there is very attractive.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name, so an example of a woman.

parts.note: Sam is a man's name
a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a university degree

explanation.surface: A graduate fellow took part in a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A lively Brazilian ballroom form is one kind of dance.

parts.note: about means regarding or concerning
ti is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale
me is the third note of the sol-fa scale, also spelt mi

explanation.surface: Talking about a pair of musical notes, someone complains of lateness.
explanation.walkthrough: TI and ME are sol-fa note names (do, re, me ... ti).
explanation.definitionFit: Said impatiently when someone finally arrives, the idiom means they should have come earlier.

clue.text: Not on the middle ground and slightly eccentric

definitions.meaning: literally placed away from the centre point
figuratively a little odd or unconventional

explanation.definitionFit: Literally positioned away from the midpoint; figuratively slightly odd, both senses of the compound.

clue.text: Incas' fate perhaps to attract attention?

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the preceding letters might be arranged another way

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material
taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: The destiny of the Inca empire might draw people's interest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' asks for a rearrangement of INCAS FATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To captivate someone is to hold and attract their attention.

clue.text: Deal with chaps on time during surgery perhaps

parts.note: to treat something is to deal with it
chaps are men

explanation.surface: Handling men on schedule in an operating theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: An operation is one form of medical care, so surgery is an example, flagged by perhaps.

parts.note: Di is short for Diana, with the possessive S
counts are continental European noblemen

explanation.surface: Princess Diana's European aristocrats are being snubbed.
explanation.definitionFit: To discount a claim is to disregard it, a verb synonym of ignore.

clue.text: Catastrophe for debutante with twisted lace

parts.note: deb is short for debutante

indicators.note: twisted says the following word's letters are wrung into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A society girl's coming-out is ruined by tangled lace on her dress.
explanation.walkthrough: A debutante is a young upper-class woman making her society debut; 'twisted' scrambles the fabric word into ACLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden, humiliating failure is a fiasco, close in sense to a catastrophe.

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times, the newspaper this puzzle appears in

explanation.surface: Is pinching this very newspaper a crime?
explanation.definitionFit: Taking another's property is stealing; this noun names the act.

clue.text: Sat up with Edward and nibbled

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: Ted is a familiar form of Edward

explanation.surface: Sitting up with a friend, someone took small bites.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sat up' reads like staying awake, but 'up' reverses the verb in this down entry, giving TAS.
explanation.definitionFit: To have nibbled is to have taken a small taste, a past-tense match.

indicators.note: wrong says the letters given are not yet in their right order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material
taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: Some people from Africa are mistaken about a steamship.
explanation.definitionFit: The Basuto people are the Sotho of Lesotho, so these are Africans.

definitions.meaning: a brawl or bout of fighting

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means discard; as a noun it is an informal word for a fight or tussle.

parts.note: puds is informal British shorthand for puddings, desserts

explanation.surface: Choosing between potatoes and little desserts.
explanation.walkthrough: PUDS is British slang for puddings, the sweet course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal slang word for potatoes, a straight colloquial synonym.

clue.text: The rascal cooked suet to provide energy

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous rascal

indicators.note: cooked suggests the next word's letters are altered or messed about

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A naughty child prepares suet to give himself a boost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' is only surface padding; 'cooked' is a common kitchen-flavoured anagram signal, turning the fat into ETUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Driving force or momentum is impetus, close to energy in everyday use.

definitions.meaning: the monk ranking next below an abbot

explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means earlier; as a noun it names an abbey's second-in-command.

indicators.note: about says one piece goes around another
new means the following word is made over in a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A fresh leaflet about the university's courses of study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges CIRCULAR, and 'about' puts it around U.
explanation.definitionFit: These are programmes of study, plural of the Latin word for a course.

parts.note: the Roman numeral I stands for one
René is a typical French man's name

explanation.surface: A single French chap's girlfriend.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name, so an example of a girl.

clue.text: Apologise from train to Reginald and rest in confusion

parts.note: an express is a fast train
Reg is short for Reginald

indicators.note: in confusion says the letters of the preceding word are muddled

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: Saying sorry for travelling by train to see Reg, then muddling the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from train' reads like travelling but is a synonym piece; 'in confusion' scrambles the last word into RETS.
explanation.definitionFit: To say sorry formally is to apologise; this phrase is the formal idiom.
